text: Find the recommended inflation pressure on the vehicle placard, commonly on the driver-side door area, or in the owner’s manual. Do not use the tire sidewall maximum as the vehicle’s recommended pressure.
Check tire pressure when tires are cold, ideally after the vehicle has been parked for at least three hours. Warm tires can show a higher pressure reading.
Check the pressure of all tires, including the spare if fitted, at least monthly and before long trips.
Underinflation can worsen handling and fuel economy, cause uneven wear, and increase the chance of tire failure.
A tire-pressure monitoring system warning means one or more tires may be significantly underinflated. Check pressure promptly; do not rely on the warning system as a substitute for routine checks.
Inspect tread and tire condition regularly, including during monthly pressure checks.
Tires have built-in treadwear indicators. When the tread becomes level with these raised indicators, the tire has reached its wear limit and should be replaced.
NHTSA guidance says tires should be replaced when tread wears down to 2/32 inch. This is U.S. guidance; check local rules and safety recommendations.

Look for cuts, cracks, bulges, punctures, or other damage on tread and sidewalls. A bulge or serious damage needs prompt professional assessment; do not continue normal driving on a visibly unsafe tire.
Rotating tires can reduce irregular wear and help extend tire life. Follow the vehicle manufacturer’s schedule and rotation pattern.
If the manufacturer recommends rotation, NHTSA cites 5,000–8,000 miles as a general interval, but the correct interval and pattern depend on the vehicle and tires.
Some vehicles or tire setups should not use a standard rotation pattern, such as certain staggered-size or directional tire arrangements. Check the owner’s manual.
Wheel balancing helps the wheel-and-tire assembly rotate smoothly and can reduce vibration. New tires should be balanced when installed.
Wheel alignment helps the vehicle track straight and supports even tire wear. If the car pulls to one side or tires wear unevenly, have alignment checked by a qualified technician.
Choose replacement tires in the size and load rating specified by the vehicle manufacturer. Check the owner’s manual or vehicle tire-information label.
Persistent tire or steering vibration, unusual noise, or repeated pressure loss should be checked by a tire professional.
A spare tire can also age and lose pressure. Check its condition and pressure as directed by the vehicle maker; a temporary spare is not a routine replacement for a worn tire.
Tires can deteriorate with age even when tread remains. Check the vehicle and tire manufacturers’ guidance on age-based replacement and inspect older tires carefully.
Overinflation can cause uneven wear and a harsher ride. Use the vehicle manufacturer’s specified cold pressure rather than guessing.
After striking a pothole or curb, inspect the tire and check pressure. If you see a bulge, cut, or other damage, seek professional inspection.
